title: Faster verify.py
eyebrow: Proposal · a verify.py rework step for the #306 restructure

short.lead: verify.py is the script that checks the plugin's hooks do what the docs say. You said it takes several minutes in a cloud session. Our rules make a session run it twice before claiming success, which doubles the wait. I timed one run here: 197 seconds for 913 checks. The approved restructure plan (#306) has no step that makes it faster. Step 2 only requires verify.py to keep passing. Step 10 only says each plugin passes its own tests. This page proposes adding a rework step for verify.py to the plan. It asks you two questions: how verify.py gets faster, and how often a session runs it.
short.hint: Tap a row to see what was measured.
items: 154 seconds (78%): verify.py starts hook.py (the script that runs the plugin's hooks) as a fresh Python process 898 times, about 0.17 seconds each.
29 seconds: 30 page builds with make_page.py (the script that builds pages like this one), including its browser check.
Under 14 seconds: everything else, such as git commands and the docs checkers.
Measured on 2026-10-21 by timing every process one verify.py run started on this branch.
Most of each hook.py start is recompiling it
Three timings: starting Python takes 0.017 seconds, one whole hook.py run takes 0.147 seconds, and compiling hook.py alone takes 0.101 seconds.
Python recompiles a script it runs directly every time, but caches the compiled form of a module it imports.
That is the existing issue #204 (Every hook call recompiles all of hook.py, about half its run time).
Step 2 removes most of the compile cost
Step 2 (#340) turns hook.py into a short dispatcher, a small script that only passes each call to the right part. Each part becomes a module that hook.py imports, so Python caches its compiled form.
Estimated saving: about 0.08 seconds on each of 898 starts, roughly 75 of the 197 seconds. It's an estimate because step 2 isn't built yet.
Nothing from you. The rework step measures this again after step 2 instead of trusting the estimate.
How verify.py gets faster, and how often it runs

choices: q1
1. Beyond step 2's saving, how does verify.py get faster?
A

Split verify.py by part, with one test file per part (core, safe git, design loop and so on) and a small runner script that runs them. In a session the runner runs the parts at the same time on the machine's cores. It can also run only the parts a change touched. CI, the check GitHub runs on every pull request, always runs every part.
Each part's tests travel with that part's plugin in step 10 anyway. Running only what changed makes a typical session check a fraction of the full run; the exact saving is measured after the split.
B
As A, and also move most hook tests from starting hook.py as a process to calling its code directly inside the test, keeping a smaller set of whole-process tests
The biggest saving, since a direct call takes milliseconds, but fewer tests run the hooks the way Claude Code really starts them.
C
Only run verify.py's existing tests in parallel, without splitting the file
Least work, but the tests don't follow the parts into their plugins in step 10.
In every option, every existing check is kept; nothing is deleted to save time.
q2
2. How often does a session run the tests?
A
In a session, run the parts a change touched twice and everything else once; CI runs the full suite on every pull request
The second run still catches a flaky test where the change is, without doubling the whole suite.
B
Run the full suite once in a session, and let CI's run be the second
Halves the session's test time, but a flaky test is only caught after the push.
C
Keep today's rule: the full suite twice in every session
No change to the rule; the saving comes only from question 1.
Your grilling answer in round 1, question 3 (how many times a suite runs before a success claim: twice, everywhere) changes under A or B, and the decisions log records the change.
